candidate_workflows: Draft normally, then test every sentence by asking whether it is how you would explain the idea to a friend; replace formal or inflated language with the spoken version.

Read the draft aloud before publishing and repair anything that sounds unlike conversation; if sentence-level revision cannot rescue it, explain the idea to someone and rebuild the draft from that explanation.
title: Write Like You Talk

candidate_workflows: Audit venture selection retrospectively by comparing subsequent performance among selected groups: if one group had to clear a higher hidden bar, its selected members should outperform, provided the outcome measure is valid and underlying ability distributions are comparable; the inference fails when the selector intentionally applies different criteria to different groups.

For startup-investment returns, preserve extreme winners in the analysis because outliers drive the portfolio outcome; excluding them can erase the very signal the selection process is meant to identify.
title: A Way to Detect Bias

candidate_workflows: Treat culture as part of the product when the organization is a community: make operating behavior authentic, consistent, and trust-building rather than imitating the formality of incumbent institutions.

At the earliest investment stage, product and growth evidence may not exist, so supplement technical questioning with rare, practiced character judgment and targeted questions that reveal team red flags; silence or assigning a generic quiet observer is not by itself a selection method.

Evaluate admissions as long-term network curation, not one transaction: reject doubtful character even when near-term success looks plausible because every accepted member changes the trust and helpfulness of the alumni community.
title: Jessica Livingston

candidate_workflows: Before decomposing a vertically integrated operation, test whether a mature specialist-supplier network can deliver the required scale and whether available technology can coordinate it; integration may be rational while the market is immature, and decomposition becomes attractive only after specialists, lower transaction costs, and replaceability make the network viable.

When entering a market dominated by a large incumbent, look for a new product category or side component that can become the customer-facing standard; treat incumbent scale and old assumptions as potential liabilities when technical change outruns economies of scale.
title: The Refragmentation

candidate_workflows: When an aggregate metric mixes beneficial and harmful mechanisms, inspect individual cases, identify the cause of each outcome, and ask what those cases would have looked like under a relevant earlier or alternative baseline before choosing an intervention.

Choose the measure that directly represents the problem to solve, then audit nearby outcomes that the metric can worsen; target the underlying user or social result instead of optimizing a convenient statistical symptom.

As startup costs fall, reassess financing leverage: use lower capital requirements to limit dilution and preserve founder board control when feasible, recognizing that cheaper formation shifts negotiating power from investors toward founders.

When judging founders, use determination chiefly to estimate survival versus failure and treat sustained mission as more relevant to the largest outcomes; do not claim to predict mission from initial posture, because founders can change after starting the company.
title: Economic Inequality

candidate_workflows: Separate waste imposed by circumstances from waste that captures attention by choice: accept that some work errands are unavoidable, but compare employers and environments by how much unnecessary meeting, bureaucracy, and posturing they impose.
For a freelancer or small company, fire or avoid a toxic customer when the reduction in wasted time is greater than the resulting loss of income.
Treat online disputes and addictive pastimes as self-chosen attention traps: step outside the defensive impulse, ask whether this is how you want to spend the time, and usually decline the argument.

When deciding whether something deserves attention, ask whether it will matter later; distrust sharp but short-lived urgency, act promptly on work and relationships that do matter, and deliberately notice the time the choice preserves.
title: Life is Short

candidate_workflows: Apply this playbook only after confirming a young-talent foothold and a first-rate research university; the source is partly Pittsburgh-specific, and the interventions do not by themselves create those starting conditions.

Treat the people creating founder-attracting amenities as users of the city: interview them about obstacles, remove concrete friction such as slow permits, and preserve the distinctive neighborhoods and affordability drawing young talent.

Build the talent base before branding an entrepreneurship program: make the research institution excellent, attract ambitious people, leave room for side projects, avoid claiming student and faculty intellectual property, and allow leaves or deferred admission.

Expect successful startups to emerge organically from founders building interesting side projects; create unstructured time and institutional permission for experiments instead of aiming vaguely at innovation.

Make broad tolerance of nonconformity an ecosystem requirement; a city cannot selectively admit only the strangeness that later produces successful startups because promising and unpromising forms are intermingled.

If local capital is scarce, exploit falling startup costs, crowdfunding, and temporary accelerator access while companies build locally; let successful founders gradually become the next investor community rather than trying to manufacture one immediately.
title: How to Make Pittsburgh a Startup Hub

candidate_workflows: Evaluate an exploratory bet using what was knowable when it was chosen, not the clarity created by its eventual outcome; bets that looked similarly plausible in advance can diverge, so a failed result does not by itself prove the original judgment was irrational.
title: The Risk of Discovery

candidate_workflows: When a builder-oriented CEO attracts criticism, account for charisma bias: power without charm can draw hostility that a more charismatic leader could disarm, so criticism alone is not sufficient proof that the CEO is wrong for the role.
title: Charisma / Power

candidate_workflows: Assess an insight on two dimensions, generality and surprise; improve a narrow observation by extracting a transferable lesson, or revisit a very general idea and search for a small true addition.

When working on general ideas, keep writing through apparent repetition and minor novelty; a different formulation can expose the useful delta, and small deltas can generate more novel follow-on ideas.
title: General and Surprising

candidate_workflows: Look for work that creates something, is intrinsically interesting, matters if successful, and is unusually tractable for the person doing it; use durable curiosity as evidence of both aptitude and the motivation to persist.

Protect exploration whose value cannot be justified in advance: follow overlooked paths that genuine interest reveals, accept that some will fail, and compare switching or hedging against the loss of depth and upside.

When blocked by a conventionally promising project, ask what you would explore for a year if importance were unlikely but interest were high; run the side project as a way to discover a new path rather than as a prestige move.

Give learners fair exposure to a subject, then let durable interest be learner-led; when they choose one, support unusually deep exploration instead of trying to manufacture enthusiasm that will not stick.
title: The Bus Ticket Theory of Genius

candidate_workflows: Map assumptions the organization treats as untouchable, then investigate good ideas that would directly or indirectly contradict them; protect the exploration from reflexive punishment because suppressing heresy also suppresses discoveries in the surrounding dead zone.
title: Novelty and Heresy

candidate_workflows: When founders search for a fundraising or launch trick, redirect the sequence to fundamentals: make the company a good investment by building a good product, get users through usefulness and recommendation, and use revenue or usage growth as the test.
Before optimizing a score or gate, ask whether it is an authority-imposed proxy that can be hacked or a direct outcome users control; prefer work where winning means producing the result itself.

If a startup plan is becoming elaborate, identify the apparent test the team is trying to game and replace it with the direct user need and observable outcome that the proxy was supposed to represent.
title: The Lesson to Unlearn

candidate_workflows: When caregiving reduces available time and attention, schedule protected work blocks, begin even when inspiration is absent, and define a stopping boundary so work cannot spill across family time.

Optionally experiment with personal commitment devices, such as framing the work around what children should know or making a concrete post-completion promise, but treat these as uncertain coping tactics rather than requirements or ways to erase the underlying attention tradeoff.
title: Having Kids

candidate_workflows: Before accepting that a field is exhausted, map whether many people have explored the same narrow region; search for a new entry into a large unfashionable area, and use genuine interest to keep working when peers mistake marginality for unimportance.
title: Fashionable Problems

candidate_workflows: Do not acquire a bundle of positions or mechanically choose the midpoint; choose which questions matter to the work, evaluate each claim independently, and accept that the resulting views may be scattered rather than ideologically consistent.

When the ideas used in the work intersect a political dispute, separate the technical question from group identity and judge it on its own evidence, including the possibility that both established sides chose the wrong question.
title: The Two Kinds of Moderate

candidate_workflows: Apply this pattern only after company growth has made founders public figures and a critic's hostility is obsessive and repeated over time; do not use it to dismiss ordinary, one-off, or product-relevant criticism.

Once repeated obsession is established, check thoughtful neutral opinion and strongly default to non-engagement; consider a narrow refutation only when a bogus claim is being used to recruit a mob, and even then err toward not responding.
title: Haters

candidate_workflows: When a new market, technology, or country creates novice discomfort, distinguish failure at a familiar task from the natural confusion of doing something novel; treat repeated local beginnerhood as evidence that the team is expanding its global knowledge rather than as a reason to retreat.
title: Being a Noob
